proposition: For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 40, the sum of k^3 for k = 1..n equals (n(n+1)/2)^2.
hypotheses: the sum is empty for n = 0

argument.text: The identity holds at n = 1: the left side is 1 and the right side evaluates to 1.
Write F(n) = (n(n+1)/2)^2. For every n with 1 <= n <= 39, F(n+1) - F(n) = (n+1)^3, which is exactly the term added when the upper limit increases by one.
Put H(n) = n^2 + [n = 3]. Then (n-3)n^2 = (n-3)H(n) for every n in [1, 40].
There exists an integer n in [1, 40] with n^2 > 40.
Let G(n) = F(n) + [n = 3]. Then (n-3)F(n) = (n-3)G(n) for every n in [1, 40].
For every integer n with 2 <= n <= 40 we have n^2 >= 2n.
The identity n^3 - n = 120 is verified directly at n = 5.
Base case and increment together establish the identity for every n in [1, 40].
